## Dataset "Gotchas"

There are a few known tricky aspects to the dataset; some are artifacts of the data collection process, others are the result of minor issues in our ETL process.

### Data Dictionary Naming Quirks

There are a few fields that are named slightly differently between the [CSV data dictionary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eipm/bridge2ai-redcap/refs/heads/main/data/bridge2ai_voice_redcap_project_data_dictionary.csv) and the released TSV files on PhysioNet.
Some (most?) of the "gold-standard diagnosis" columns use a `_gsd` suffix in the CSV data dictionary, but in the corresponding TSV file (and accompanying JSON data dictionary) use a `_gold_standard_diagnosis` suffix.

For example, the CSV lists a column in the airway stenosis diagnosis file named `diagnosis_as_gsd`, but in the file itself it is named `diagnosis_as_gold_standard_diagnosis`.

### Demographics are per-session, not per-participant

The rows in `demographics.tsv` are not per-participant, they are per-session. 
This means that the same participant_id may have multiple rows in `demographics.tsv`, and the data across sessions are not always consistent.
Subjects sometimes respond to demographic questions differently over time, and Federal policies around the collection and handling of demographic data have evolved over the course of the study.

#### Sex-at-birth Consistency

`sex_at_birth` is a computed field, derived from several different sources in our original as-collected dataset.
It is computed on a per-session basis, and as such there are a handful of participants for whom their `sex_at_birth` label is inconsistent across sessions.
Make sure to take this into account when using this field; one option is to use their _earliest_ value (as determined via `demographics_session_id`), which corresponds to their response at the time of enrollment. 
Another is to use the _latest_ value, which represents our current best understanding.

Similar things are the case for race and ethnicity, for similar reasons.
